cards.explanation: The answer is the signs and wonders the Most High did for him. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, writes, “I am pleased to declare the signs and wonders that the Most High God has performed for me.” Look at whose work he's reporting, friends. It's the Most High's, and the king isn't taking a bow for any of it.

The answer is True. Nebuchadnezzar says of the Most High, “His kingdom is an eternal kingdom; His dominion endures from generation to generation.” That's a man who runs a huge kingdom himself, calling someone else's kingdom the one that lasts. I'd say that's a good line to put at the top of a letter.

The answer is frightened. The king says, “I had a dream, and it frightened me; while I was in my bed, the images and visions in my mind alarmed me.” He was lying in bed, and the dream still got to him. Nobody walks away from a dream like that saying, "Well, that was nice."

The answer is False. The king says that when he told the magicians, enchanters, astrologers and diviners the dream, “…they could not interpret it for me.” A whole room of them came up empty. That's a long line of experts with nothing to say.

The answer is the spirit of the holy gods. The king tells Daniel, “…I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in you and that no mystery baffles you.” Those are the king's own words about Daniel. He brings the dream to Daniel after the other wise men could not interpret it (Daniel 4:7).

The answers are shelter and fed. The king says, “Under it the beasts of the field found shelter…” and “…from it every creature was fed.” He also says “…upon it was food for all.” That's a tree big enough that the animals just move in under it, and I'd like a cookie jar that popular. This tree wasn't just tall, friends, it was taking care of everybody. Birds nested in its branches too.

The answer is cut it down. The watcher calls out in a loud voice, “Cut down the tree and chop off its branches; strip off its leaves and scatter its fruit.” After that long description of a great tree, this is a hard turn. The watcher doesn't whisper it either.

The answer is False. The watcher says, “But leave the stump with its roots in the ground, with a band of iron and bronze around it, in the tender grass of the field.” The stump and its roots stay in the ground. It's a tree that's been cut down and still isn't finished.

The answer is so the living know the Most High rules. The decree is declared “…so that the living will know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind and gives it to whom He wishes…” The holy ones state the purpose themselves. It's about who is really in charge.

The answer is that the king tells Daniel not to let the dream alarm him. Daniel, whom the king calls Belteshazzar, is perplexed, so the king says, “Belteshazzar, do not let the dream or its interpretation alarm you.” Here's the man who was alarmed by the dream, telling someone else not to be. I think that's a kind thing to say, even if it's a little funny.

The answer is enemies. Daniel says, “My lord, may the dream apply to those who hate you, and its interpretation to your enemies!” I think he's softening hard news before he says it. That's how it sounds to me, anyway.

The answer is King Nebuchadnezzar himself. Daniel says it straight to his face, “…you, O king, are that tree! For you have become great and strong; your greatness has grown to reach the sky, and your dominion extends to the ends of the earth.” The tree that grew large and strong, with its top in the sky, is the king. Daniel doesn't dance around it.

The answer is True. Daniel says, “This is the interpretation, O king, and this is the decree that the Most High has issued against my lord the king…” He doesn't say it's his own idea or the stars' idea. He names the Most High as the one who issued it.

The answers are mankind and grass. Daniel says, “You will be driven away from mankind, and your dwelling will be with the beasts of the field.” The king is going to be pushed out from among people, quite a change for a man whose letter began by greeting the whole earth. Then Daniel says, “You will feed on grass like an ox and be drenched with the dew of heaven…” An ox, friends. I've had some rough days in my day, but I never had to graze.

The answer is kingdom. Daniel says, “As for the command to leave the stump of the tree with its roots, your kingdom will be restored to you as soon as you acknowledge that Heaven rules.” The stump left in the ground is the promise inside the bad news. It's a small piece of hope.

The answer is to turn from sin and show mercy to the oppressed. Daniel says, “Break away from your sins by doing what is right, and from your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed. Perhaps there will be an extension of your prosperity.” He gives the king something to do, not just a warning. He gives it right to the king's face.

The answer is that he built it all by his own power. The king exclaims, “Is this not Babylon the Great, which I myself have built as a royal residence by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” Count the "my" words in that sentence, friends. It's a lot of me for one rooftop.

The answer is True. The voice says, “It is decreed to you, King Nebuchadnezzar, that the kingdom has departed from you.” It comes while the words are still in his mouth. There's no pause between the boast and the answer.
The answer is False. The text says, “At that moment the sentence against Nebuchadnezzar was fulfilled.” It happened right then, with no waiting. He had already had his twelve months.

The answer is that his sanity is restored to him. The king says, “…at the end of those days I, Nebuchadnezzar, looked up to heaven, and my sanity was restored to me.” Then he praises the Most High. It starts with him looking up.

The answer is False, and that's the good news. The king says, “My advisers and nobles sought me out, and I was restored to my throne, and surpassing greatness was added to me.” They came looking for him, and the throne is waiting. It's a very different ending from the one he walked into.

The answer is that the King of heaven is able to humble those who walk in pride. That's the king's closing line, “And He is able to humble those who walk in pride.” He's not guessing. He's speaking from what happened to him, and I think that's why it lands.
